Quick Read

Supermicro (SMCI) raised its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook to as much as $82 billion, yet shares sank 29% in a month on smuggling probe fears.

Supermicro trades near 3x forward earnings while Dell (DELL) and HPE (HPE) fetch about 9x, a gap the article blames on legal risk.

Gross margin fell to 12.7% as low-margin AI projects grew, and one customer accounted for 44% of revenue.

Read: Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps with, and it is free today. Read more here.

Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) now says fiscal 2027 revenue could reach $82 billion, but the stock still trades near the bottom of its 52-week range. Our 24/7 Wall St. price target is $27.18 over the next 12 months. That is 7% above the current price.

The model was set at the prior $21.65 close, where it implied 25.55% upside. Monday's rebound has already closed much of that gap. We have high confidence because earnings momentum is strong. The upside is modest because legal risk keeps the valuation multiple low.

A Record Quarter Got Buried by a 28.59% Monthly Slide

The stock is down 28.59% over the past month, 5.45% over the past week and 13.22% year to date. Its 52-week range runs from $19.48 to $51.40. The selloff came after a strong report.

On November 3, Supermicro posted revenue of $19.9 billion, up 298% year over year. Non-GAAP EPS of $1.81 beat the $1.2346 estimate. Management also raised the fiscal 2027 outlook to $72 billion to $82 billion.

Shares fell anyway after Bloomberg reported that Manhattan prosecutors are looking into whether parties tied to Alice Huang smuggled Supermicro servers into China.

title: Dell’s Operating Costs Fell to “the Lowest in Our Company’s 42-Year History.” The Stock Fell Anyway

Dell’s Operating Costs Fell to “the Lowest in Our Company’s 42-Year History.” The Stock Fell Anyway
Rexielyn Diaz
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 10:59 PM PST 4 min read
DELL
SMCI
HPE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Dell's Operating Costs Fell to "the Lowest in Our Company's 42-Year History." The Stock Fell Anyway ©@tuu-sitthikorns-images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Dell's revenue more than doubled to $54.9 billion in its fiscal third quarter, and operating expenses fell to 7% of revenue, a record low.

Lower costs are carrying Dell's margins as low-margin AI servers grow.

The risks are a gross margin held up by price increases and a server surge that may have come early, questions Super Micro Computer and Hewlett Packard Enterprise face too.

At 8.9x forward earnings, Dell prices in a much sharper drop in profits than its guidance shows.

Dell Technologies (DELL:NYSE) just reported the kind of quarter AI bulls hope for: record revenue, up 103%, and adjusted EPS of $9.45, up 265%.

But the line that jumped out at me came from CEO Jeff Clarke on Dell's third-quarter call:

"Operating expenses were 7% of revenue, the lowest in our company's 42-year history."

The stock fell 12% on report day, and it has lost about a third of its value in the past month. Investors are asking Dell and its rivals Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE:NYSE) what happens to margins as low-margin AI server racks take over more of their sales.

But I think the market is missing how Dell is building its margin.

The earnings keep going up

Dell raised its outlook for the year ending January 2027, and its AI server backlog hit a record $132.3 billion. Analysts expect adjusted EPS to climb from $29.87 this year to $34.43 in the year ending January 2028:

Dell Technologies (DELL): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2028 (years to January) (TIKR)

That's about 15% growth, in line with the 15%-plus yearly EPS growth Dell has targeted since its October 2025 investor day.

TIKR tracks 29 analysts on Dell Technologies. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Dell Technologies, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Dell Technologies' Analyst Ratings

Costs are carrying the margin

Dell's GAAP gross margin fell from 23.6% in fiscal 2024 to 20.0% in fiscal 2026 as AI servers grew, and management holds those servers to a mid-single-digit operating margin.

Yet Dell's operating margin has climbed every year for five years:

Dell Technologies (DELL): operating (EBIT) margin (%), fiscal 2022-2026 (years to January) (TIKR)

Dell cut costs to get there: its GAAP operating expenses fell 7% from fiscal 2024 to fiscal 2026, to $14.6 billion, while revenue grew 28%.

CFO David Kennedy called the savings "sticky" and "structural," and he expects the full-year operating margin to rise about 3.5 points "despite the mix pressure of $78 billion in AI server revenue, more than 3x larger than last year."

title: Mohamed El-Erian Says Nvidia Is “Too Big to Wobble.” Its Customers’ Data Center Plans Aren’t
detail:
Mohamed El-Erian Says Nvidia Is “Too Big to Wobble.” Its Customers’ Data Center Plans Aren’t
Gian Estrada
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 9:48 PM PST 4 min read
NVDA
MSFT
SMCI
META
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Mohamed El-Erian Says Nvidia Is "Too Big to Wobble." Its Customers' Data Center Plans Aren't ©@Sergei Starostin from Pexels via Canva, @Nana Dua from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

NVIDIA gave back about 40% of its post-Huang rally this week and trades at about 10x forward earnings, despite open backing from the Trump administration.

Mohamed El-Erian says NVIDIA is "too big to wobble," but agreed 2027 looks tough for the data center build-out.

Orders haven't slipped yet, so Meta's 2027 spending plan in late January is the next test.

NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) has given back about 40% of the rally that followed Jensen Huang's return as CEO this week, even with the Trump administration openly on its side.

The bigger question is its customers. Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) spent $116 billion on capex in fiscal 2026, Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) plans $135 billion to $145 billion this year, and server maker Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) expects as much as $82 billion of sales this fiscal year.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on CNBC's Squawk Pod: "NVIDIA is structurally important. And so we have to make sure that that company remains on top."

On CNBC's Squawk on the Street, Allianz chief economic adviser Mohamed El-Erian was asked whether government policy will now steer NVIDIA. He said "that's going too far," then added: "I think we've learned that NVIDIA is too big to wobble, not to fail, simply to wobble."

Then the host listed the headwinds: "you got the Fed fighting the build out, you got Congress fighting the build out, you'll have national security regulators fighting the build out, and then you'll have the credit market fighting the build out. That's a tough picture going into 27."

El-Erian's answer? "It is."

Analysts Are Counting on NVIDIA's Spenders

Analysts expect total revenue to grow nearly 5x, from $216 billion in the year ended January 2026 to $1.07 trillion in the year ending January 2030:

NVDA Revenue, Actual and Consensus Estimates: FY2026-FY2030 (TIKR)

Microsoft shows what that growth takes from customers. Its $116 billion of capex is up from $23.9 billion in fiscal 2022:

MSFT Capital Expenditures: FY2022-FY2026 (TIKR)
The First Cracks Are Small

Orders are holding. Super Micro's revenue for the quarter ended Sept. 30 was $19.9 billion, up from $5.0 billion a year earlier.

National security rules have already reached it: after a US chip rule took effect on Nov. 19, NVIDIA reportedly told server makers, Super Micro included, to stop shipping to four Southeast Asian countries. Congress wants more: Republicans joined Democrats in criticizing Huang's return, and Sen. Tom Cotton vowed tougher chip export controls.

The credit market moves slower, and Meta shows that risk best. Its third-quarter capex of $34.9 billion was more than the $32.8 billion of cash its operations brought in. El-Erian's worry: "you'd hope, for example, that government borrowing would decline to make room for tech borrowing without pushing yields higher. That didn't happen."
